lessons.title: Source code, compilation, linking, and execution
lessons.passage: Preprocessing handles lines such as #include <stdio.h>, which brings in descriptions of available functions. The compiler checks your C and translates it into an object file, one piece of the program. The linker connects that piece to library code such as printf. Together, these steps build the program. Here the result is WebAssembly: a binary program format the browser can run. A local build can instead produce an executable for your computer.

lessons.title: Integers, floating-point numbers, characters, and Boolean values
lessons.passage: int represents whole numbers, while double represents floating-point approximations. char is an integer type used for character-sized storage; a character literal such as 'A' uses single quotes. In C17, include <stdbool.h> to use bool, true, and false. Integer widths and plain-char signedness are implementation choices within the standard’s requirements. Do not assume one compiler’s sizes describe all C platforms. The language also provides short, long, long long, and unsigned integer variants, and float and long double for other floating-point ranges or precision. This introduction uses double for fractional calculations. A float argument to printf is promoted to double; scanf follows different format rules, so do not transfer printf formats to input functions without checking their contracts.

lessons.title: Operators and precedence
lessons.passage: Multiplication, division, and remainder bind more tightly than addition and subtraction. When both operands of division are integers, the result is an integer truncated toward zero: 7 / 2 is 3. The remainder operator % works on integers; for these positive operands, 7 % 2 is 1. Division by zero is invalid. Evaluation order is a separate issue from precedence: grouping does not generally tell you the order in which unrelated function calls or side effects are evaluated.

lessons.title: Conversions, casts, and integer promotions
lessons.passage: In a mixed expression involving double and an ordinary integer, the integer can be converted to double before arithmetic. A cast explicitly requests a conversion. Signed/unsigned combinations have additional conversion rules, so avoid mixing them casually when testing ranges. Part 7’s numeric-boundary lessons revisit promotions and signed/unsigned comparisons with checked interfaces after functions and pointers have been introduced.
